summary: Defines the View-based Access Control Model for SNMP, which controls who may read or change which pieces of management information. It specifies the elements of procedure and includes a MIB to configure the model remotely. It replaces RFC 2575.

plainLanguage.summary: Not everyone should be allowed to open every drawer. This note lets an administrator decide which users can see or change which parts of a network device.

questions: what is a mib view in snmp
how does snmp access control work
subtitle: How an SNMP device decides who may read, change or be notified about which pieces of its management data.

tldr.problem: An SNMP entity holds management data that must not be open to everyone. It needs a standard way to decide, for each request, whether a given principal may read, write or receive a particular object.
tldr.mechanism: VACM maps a security model and security name to a group, then looks up that group's access entry for the context, security model and security level. The entry names a read, write and notify MIB view, and the object is checked against the view's included and excluded subtrees.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard (STD 62) and replaced RFC 2575. The MIB it defines lets the whole policy be configured remotely.

today: RFC 3415 is an Internet Standard (STD 62) and obsoletes RFC 2575. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Where VACM Fits
sections.content:
In the SNMP architecture of RFC 3411, an engine is made of a Dispatcher, a Message Processing Subsystem, a Security Subsystem and an Access Control Subsystem. The Access Control Subsystem checks whether a specific type of access (read, write or notify) to a particular object instance is allowed. RFC 3415 defines one model for it, the View-based Access Control Model (VACM), and notes that it is not necessarily the only one.

Applications call VACM; it does not call itself. A command responder applies access control to Read-Class and Write-Class requests, and a notification originator applies it when generating Notification-Class messages. It is the application's job to make the proper service calls. The policy is kept in the engine's Local Configuration Datastore, and the MIB module in this document makes parts of that datastore reachable as managed objects.
sections.plainLanguage: VACM is the door guard of an SNMP device. Other programs ask the guard 'may this person do this?' and the guard checks the guest list.

sections.title: Groups, Levels and Contexts
sections.content:
A group is a set of zero or more <securityModel, securityName> pairs, and it defines the access rights of all of them. A given securityModel and securityName pair maps to at most one group. VACM assumes the securityName has already been authenticated as needed and does no authentication of its own.

Rights can differ by security level: noAuthNoPriv, authNoPriv and authPriv. A context is a collection of management information that an entity can reach, and the same item may exist in more than one context. The vacmContextTable lists the contexts available locally by name.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of writing a rule for every person, you put people into clubs and give each club its own rules. The rules can also depend on how strong the lock on the connection is.

sections.title: MIB Views and Subtree Families
sections.content:
To restrict a group to a subset of the data, access to a context goes through a MIB view, which lists specific managed object types, and optionally specific instances. A view is built from view subtrees: all instances sharing a common OBJECT IDENTIFIER prefix. A simple view can be a single subtree, while a view such as everything relevant to one network interface is the union of several.

To avoid needing many nearly identical subtrees, such as one per column of a table row, VACM defines a family of view subtrees: an OBJECT IDENTIFIER (the family name) plus a bit string (the family mask). A mask bit of 1 means that sub-identifier must match, and 0 is a wild card. A mask shorter than needed is implicitly extended with ones, so a zero-length mask means a single subtree. A family can be included in or excluded from a view.

A group's rights for a context, security model and security level are given by three views: a read-view, a write-view and a notify-view.
sections.plainLanguage: A view is a window that shows only some rooms of a big building. A mask lets you say 'show every room on every floor but only the third door', without listing each one.

sections.title: The isAccessAllowed Decision
sections.content:
The abstract service is isAccessAllowed, taking securityModel, securityName, securityLevel, viewType (read, write or notify), contextName and variableName (the OID). It returns one status. The steps are:

  • Look up the context in vacmContextTable; if absent, return noSuchContext.
  • Map securityModel and securityName to a group in vacmSecurityToGroupTable; if absent, return noGroupName.
  • Find the entry in vacmAccessTable for the group, context, securityModel and securityLevel; if absent, return noAccessEntry.
  • Pick the read, write or notify view by viewType. An empty view name or no configured view gives noSuchView.
  • If the object instance is not in that view, return notInView; otherwise return accessAllowed.

Inside the view, the entries for that view name in vacmViewTreeFamilyTable are compared with the object. If none match, it is not in the view. If several match, the entry whose subtree has the most sub-identifiers decides whether it is included or excluded.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard asks: is this place on my list? Is this person in a club? Does the club have rules for this kind of lock? Is this particular room in the window they may look through? Any 'no' stops the check.

sections.title: The VACM Configuration MIB
sections.content:
The SNMP-VIEW-BASED-ACM-MIB has four tables and an advisory lock. vacmContextTable lists available contexts; it must be accessible via the default context. vacmSecurityToGroupTable maps a securityModel and securityName to a vacmGroupName. vacmAccessTable is indexed by group name, context prefix, security model and security level, and each row holds vacmAccessReadViewName, vacmAccessWriteViewName and vacmAccessNotifyViewName. vacmViewTreeFamilyTable holds each view's subtree, mask and an included or excluded type.

Access rows can match a context exactly or by prefix, which gives a simple form of wildcarding. The security level in a row is a minimum, where noAuthNoPriv is less than authNoPriv, which is less than authPriv. When several rows could apply, a matching security model beats any, a matching context prefix is preferred, longer prefixes win, and then the highest security level is chosen.

vacmViewSpinLock is an advisory lock for command generators editing views, and is not enforced. The MIB advises creating the excluded entries first and then the included ones, and deleting included first and then excluded. Instance-level view entries are optional.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard's lists are stored in tables that an administrator can edit from far away: a list of rooms, a list of who is in which club, a list of club rules, and a list of what each window shows.

sections.title: Initial Configuration
sections.content:
An authoritative engine that supports VACM SHOULD be configured at installation with one of three choices: initial-minimum-security-configuration, initial-semi-security-configuration or initial-no-access-configuration. The last has no initial configuration at all.

The other two share a default context named with the empty string, and a group called initial holding the USM (security model 3) name initial. That group gets three kinds of access. At noAuthNoPriv it gets the restricted view for read and notify and no write view. At authNoPriv it gets the internet view (subtree 1.3.6.1) for read, write and notify. If privacy is supported, authPriv gets the same internet view.

The restricted view is the whole internet subtree in the minimum configuration. In the semi-secure configuration it is the union of five subtrees: system, snmp, snmpEngine, snmpMPDStats and usmStats.
sections.plainLanguage: When a new device is set up, it comes with a starter rule: strangers can peek at a few harmless things, and people who prove who they are can see and change more.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
VACM decides by context, group, security model, security level, operation and view, and it assumes the calling module has already ensured the authentication and privacy required by the securityLevel passed in. Changing the view table in the wrong order can grant unwanted access in the meantime, so the recommended sequence matters.

Grouping by security model and security name does not consider security level. The RFC therefore warns that an administrator must use the securityLevel index in vacmAccessTable to separate noAuthNoPriv access from authNoPriv and authPriv access. The MIB controls access to all MIB data on the engine and may be sensitive, so both reading and writing it should be closely controlled. To be conformant, an implementation MUST implement the MIB according to vacmMIBCompliance and SHOULD implement the initial configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard trusts that someone else already checked each person's ID, so the rules must clearly say what a person who showed no ID may do. And the guest list itself must be guarded.

items.desc: A view was found but the object is not in it.

items.label: No view
items.desc: No view is configured for the requested view type.

items.desc: No vacmContextTable entry for the context name.

items.desc: No group mapping for the security model and name.

items.desc: No vacmAccessTable entry for the combination.
